revealWordProblem.title: (Review from 8.3) Apply: Water Parks
revealWordProblem.text: Andrew and his friends want to visit a waterpark, but Andrew must take his younger sister who is 8 years old and can only ride waterslides that are less than 100 feet high. Which waterpark should they visit? Include the heights of the slides at the two parks in your recommendation.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Splash Lagoon's slides are 135 ft, 105 ft, 100 ft, 80 ft, and 75 ft. Only 80 ft and 75 ft are less than 100 ft, so 2 of its 5 slides work for Andrew's sister. Wild Bay Waterpark's slides are 128 ft, 120 ft, 108 ft, and 68 ft. Only 68 ft is less than 100 ft, so just 1 of its 4 slides works for her. Since Splash Lagoon has more slides Andrew's sister is allowed to ride (2 versus 1), Andrew and his friends should visit Splash Lagoon.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 8.1–8.3
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 8.1: If you expect the answers to vary, it is a statistical question. • 8.2: Mean = add then divide, median = the middle of the ordered numbers, mode = the value that shows up most. • 8.3: MAD = the average of how far each number is from the mean (always a positive distance).

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 8.1 — Statistical Questions and Data: If you expect the answers to vary, it is a statistical question.
Lesson 8.2 — Mean, Median, and Mode: Mean = add then divide, median = the middle of the ordered numbers, mode = the value that shows up most.
Lesson 8.3 — Mean Absolute Deviation: MAD = the average of how far each number is from the mean (always a positive distance).

summaryRow.label: MAD = Sum of Absolute Deviations ÷ Number of Values

discourse.prompt: Player A's MAD is 2.4 points. If Player B's MAD is 7.2 points, what does that tell you about their consistency?
discourse.sentenceFrame: Player A has a ___ MAD, which means their scores are ___ to the mean. Player B has a ___ MAD, which means their scores are ___ from the mean. The more consistent player is ___ because ___.

optional.instructions: (Lesson 8.1) Drag each scouting question into the right bin. A statistical question expects answers that VARY from player to player; a non-statistical question has one fixed answer.

items.text: How many push-ups can each player on the team do in one minute?
How many points does each starter average per game?
How many seconds does each player take to sprint the court?
How many free throws did each teammate make in practice?
How many players are allowed on the court at once?
What is the diameter of an official basketball hoop?
How many quarters are played in one game?

optional.stem: (Lesson 8.2) A player scored 4, 8, 6, 10, and 2 points across five quarters. What is the MEAN number of points?
optional.explanation: Add the points: 4 + 8 + 6 + 10 + 2 = 30. Divide by 5 quarters: 30 ÷ 5 = 6.
choiceFeedback: Did you divide by something other than the number of quarters?
This is the sum—does the mean equal the sum?
The highest score is 10—is that the average of all the scores?

optional.stem: (Lesson 8.3) A guard scored 2, 4, 6, 8 points in four scrimmages, so the mean is 5 points. The distances from the mean are 3, 1, 1, 3. What is the mean absolute deviation (MAD)?
optional.explanation: Add the distances: 3 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 8. Divide by the 4 games: 8 ÷ 4 = 2. The MAD is 2 points.
choiceFeedback: Mean is 5, not the distances—use the distances for MAD.
Did you divide by the number of values (4)?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 8.1) Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many points did each player score this season?
How many points are scored for a free throw?
What sport does this team play?
How many halves are in a soccer game?
approaching.explanation: "How many points did each player score?" is statistical because different players will have different scores — there is variability in the data.
choiceFeedback: A free throw's points are fixed—does this question ask about variation?
What sport is played doesn't vary—do different people answer this differently?
Halves in a game is a rule—does it change from one observation to another?
hints: Re-read each question and ask: would different people or games give different answers, or is there just one fixed answer?
A statistical question expects variability — many answers that differ. Sort each choice into 'one fixed answer' or 'answers that vary'.
Test one: 'How many halves are in a soccer game?' Every game has the same number — no variability there. Check the other three the same way.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 8.1) Which question is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many innings are in a baseball game?
How many home runs did each player hit this year?
How many miles does each runner train per week?
How tall is each player on the basketball team?
approaching.explanation: "How many innings are in a baseball game?" has one fixed answer (9) — no variability. The other questions all produce different answers for different people.
choiceFeedback: Each player hit a different number of home runs—would the answer vary?
Different runners train different miles—would the data vary?
Each player has a different height—would the answers vary?
hints: Careful — this asks for the question that is NOT statistical: the one with a single fixed answer instead of varying data.
For each choice ask: 'Would each player or runner give a different number?' The odd one out is a rule of the game, not data you collect.
Start with 'How tall is each player?' — heights differ player to player, so that one IS statistical. Keep testing until one has just one answer.

choiceFeedback: Add the numbers first—does 14 equal the sum divided by 5?
Did you forget to divide by the count of numbers?
Is 60 the mean, or the sum?
hints: Mean means the average of all five numbers — you'll need both a total and how many numbers there are.
Use the formula: mean = sum of the values ÷ how many values. Count first: there are 5 numbers here.
Step 1: add 10 + 14 + 8 + 12 + 16 to get the total. Then divide that total by 5 — the result is the mean.

choiceFeedback: Did you order them first? What's the middle value after ordering?
The lowest is 3—is median always the lowest?
7 is not the middle value—order them first.
hints: Median = the middle number, but only AFTER the list is in order. Don't pick the middle of the unsorted list.
Rewrite 3, 7, 2, 9, 5 from least to greatest, then count in from both ends until you reach the one value in the exact middle.
Start ordering: the smallest is 2, then 3... finish the ordered list of all five values, then circle the 3rd one — that's the median.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 8.3) The mean of a data set is 15. One value is 11. What is the absolute deviation of that value from the mean?
choiceFeedback: Absolute deviation is always positive—take the absolute value of 11 − 15.
The deviation is negative; absolute deviation is the positive version.
Absolute means positive—what's |11 − 15|?
hints: Absolute deviation asks: how FAR is the value 11 from the mean of 15? A distance is always a positive number.
Subtract: value − mean gives the deviation. Then take the absolute value (drop any negative sign) to get the absolute deviation.
Step 1: set up 11 − 15 (the result will be negative). Step 2 is turning that result into a positive distance.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 8.3) A data set has absolute deviations of 3, 1, 5, 2, 4. What is the MAD?
choiceFeedback: Did you find the largest deviation instead of the average?
Add them all and divide by the count of values, not just sum them.
The largest is 5—is MAD the maximum deviation?
hints: You're given the five absolute deviations already — no subtracting needed. MAD is their average.
MAD = (sum of the absolute deviations) ÷ (how many there are). Count them: there are 5 deviations listed.
Step 1: add 3 + 1 + 5 + 2 + 4. Step 2: divide that total by 5. Don't stop after adding — the sum alone is not the MAD.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 8.1) A coach asks: "How many hours does each athlete on the track team sleep the night before a meet?" Why is this a statistical question?
choices: Because the answers will vary from athlete to athlete
Because it has a numerical answer
onLevel.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability. Different athletes sleep different amounts, so the data collected will vary.
choiceFeedback: Sports is a topic—what specific part makes this statistical?
Numbers can appear in fixed-answer questions too—why is this different?
Who asks the question doesn't determine if it's statistical—look deeper.
hints: Notice the words 'each athlete' — the coach plans to collect one number from every runner on the team.
Ask: will all athletes report the same hours of sleep? What we call it when collected answers differ is the key to this question.
Imagine the coach's list: 8, 6.5, 9, 7 hours from different athletes. The first step is naming what a changing list like that shows.

rows.question: How many push-ups can each student do in one minute?
rows.why: Different students can do different amounts — there is variability.

rows.question: How many sides does a basketball court have?
rows.why: There is one fixed answer (4 sides) — no variability.

rows.question: How far does each player kick the ball?
rows.why: Different players kick different distances — the data varies.

onLevel.label: (Lesson 8.1) Decide if each question is statistical and explain why.
hints: For each row, check whether the question asks about many people ('each student', 'each player') or one fixed fact about the game.
Column 2: write Yes if answers would differ person to person, No if there's only one possible answer. Column 3: explain using 'varies' or 'fixed'.
Row 1: push-ups in one minute — could two students do different amounts? Write Yes or No, then explain why in the last column.
Each row needs three different measures: mean (average), median (middle of the ordered list), and mode (most frequent value).
Do one row at a time: add and divide by the count for mean; reorder the list for median; tally repeats for mode. Round means to 2 decimals.
Row 1 (5, 8, 8, 10, 14): add the five values and divide by 5 for the mean. The list is already ordered, so the median is the 3rd value.
onLevel.title: (Lesson 8.2) Review problem

onLevel.label: (Lesson 8.2) Match each measure to its definition.
hints: These are the four core vocabulary words of this unit — each pairs with a short formula or phrase that defines it.
Use word clues: 'mean' is the average (uses ÷), 'median' sounds like 'middle', 'mode' starts like 'most', 'range' is how far the data reaches.
Start with Median: 'med-' is like 'middle' — pair it with the middle-value card, then match the remaining three by their clues.
The mean is 10. Column 2 asks for Score − 10 (keep negative signs!). Column 3 drops the sign to make each a distance.
Work row by row: 12 − 10, then 8 − 10, and so on. For the MAD at the end: add ALL five absolute deviations and divide by 5.
Row 1: 12 − 10 = 2, and |2| = 2. Now do 8 − 10 the same way — careful, this one comes out negative before you take the absolute value.
onLevel.title: (Lesson 8.3) Review problem

onLevel.label: (Lesson 8.3) Match each MAD value to what it tells you about the data.
hints: MAD is spread: 'on average, how far are the values from the mean?' A bigger MAD means the data wanders farther.
Order the four MADs first: 0, 1.5, 4.2, 8.0. Then match: smallest → tightest data, largest → most spread out.
Start with MAD = 0: an average distance of zero means no value is ever away from the mean. Find the card that describes data like that.

extending.title: (Lesson 8.1) Find the Reasoning Error

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?

workedExample.label: Student says
workedExample.work: This is NOT a statistical question.

workedExample.label: Reason
workedExample.work: It only asks about one player, so there is no variability.

extending.correctWork: Even though it asks about one player, "this season" means multiple games. The number of touchdowns per game varies, so there IS variability in the data. This IS a statistical question.
hints: Think about whether the data collected would have different values across games.
The question asks about performance over a whole season — each game can have a different result.

extending.title: (Lesson 8.2) Find the Stats Error
extending.correctWork: Mode = 15 (appears twice, more than any other value). Mode is the most frequent value, not the largest.
hints: Mode means 'most often,' not 'most.' Which number appears the most times?
15 appears twice. No other number repeats. So the mode is 15, not 18.

extending.title: (Lesson 8.3) Find the MAD Error
extending.correctWork: You must use absolute values of the deviations: |−10| = 10, |−5| = 5, |0| = 0, |5| = 5, |10| = 10. MAD = (10 + 5 + 0 + 5 + 10) ÷ 5 = 30 ÷ 5 = 6.
hints: MAD stands for Mean ABSOLUTE Deviation. What does 'absolute' mean you need to do?
Take the absolute value of each deviation before adding them: |−10| = 10, |−5| = 5, etc.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Mean Absolute Deviation is adding the signed deviations (value − mean) instead of their absolute values, so the positives and negatives cancel out to 0. For 6, 8, 10, 12 (mean = 9), the deviations are −3, −1, 1, 3 — they sum to 0, but that is NOT the MAD. Before averaging, take the absolute value of every deviation so each becomes a positive distance: |−3| = 3, |−1| = 1, |1| = 1, |3| = 3. Sum = 8, so MAD = 8 ÷ 4 = 2. A MAD of exactly 0 is a warning sign — it only happens if every value in the data set equals the mean.

diagram.title: Same Mean, Different Spread — MAD of Goals Allowed
diagram.caption: Both keepers average 1.67 goals per game. Keeper A's smaller MAD (0.67) means each game stays closer to that average — Keeper B swings between shutouts and 4-goal games.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 8.2) Data set: 4, 7, 10, 7, 12. What is the median?
choiceFeedback: Order the values first, then find the exact middle one.
The median is the middle of the ORDERED list, not the largest.
Sort the numbers and pick the center — 4 is the smallest.
hints: Median means middle — but the list 4, 7, 10, 7, 12 isn't in order yet. That's your first job.
Rewrite the five values from least to greatest, then count in one value at a time from each end until you meet in the middle.
Start the ordered list: 4 is the smallest value. Keep placing values least to greatest, then circle the 3rd of the 5 — that position is the median.
